title: Orsen and the Hymn
premise: Juniper Villalobos takes a teaching post in the dying town of Orsen, where eleven students vanished decades ago and the school board forbids any mention of them. When a road crew unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, Juniper's obsessive documentation begins recording things that haven't happened yet, and the vanished children start appearing in attendance logs. The truth: the town's founding families invited something in to bury a crime, and it has been keeping the children 'safe' ever since. Juniper must choose between the law that protects the guilty families and a hymn only the dead remember, ending with Juniper leading the children out at sunrise while the town's elders are left to answer the door themselves.
about_author: Jonah Coldharbour is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in towns too small for their own records offices. They write horror about paperwork, small communities, and the things that survive in the gaps between them.

chapters.title: Attendance Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Juniper Villalobos arrives in Orsen and takes over a classroom with eleven empty desks no one will explain. Told through Juniper's journal entries, the chapter establishes the town's polite evasions and Juniper's compulsive record-keeping. The emotional beat is wary loneliness: a person who believes that writing things down keeps them real.

chapters.title: Eleven Desks, Ten Students
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. A student, Marisol, quietly tells Juniper the eleventh desk belongs to 'the girl who waits.' That night, the attendance ledger shows a name Juniper never wrote: Ada Kettle, marked present in Juniper's own handwriting. The beat is creeping doubt—Juniper's faith in documentation begins to curdle into fear of it.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Alternating between Juniper and foreman Dale Ostrander's rough field log, the crew digging the new road unearths a cellar door beneath the schoolyard, bolted from the inside. Dale reports it; the school board orders it reburied by morning. The beat is institutional dread—the town moves like a body defending itself.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Remembers
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Cross-referencing old records, Juniper finds the 1974 class photo: eleven children, one face scratched out, and a hymn sheet with verses that continue past where any hymn should end. Marisol stops coming to school. The beat is grief sharpening into resolve—Juniper decides someone has to keep the record honest.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Told partly through the Kettle family patriarch's brittle recollections, the chapter reveals the 1974 fire at the Kettle mill, the eleven children who died locked inside, and the ritual the elders performed to keep the town 'quiet.' The beat is complicity—justice was traded for peace, and everyone signed.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, night. The reburied door stands open in the schoolyard, soil thrown outward. Juniper descends and finds the classroom from 1974 preserved below—eleven desks, a hymn on the chalkboard, and Ada Kettle's voice asking who finally came to take attendance. The beat is terrible recognition: the children were never missing. They were kept.

chapters.title: Lockdown
chapters.summary: Multiple close POVs—Juniper, Dale, and board chair Ruth Kettle—as the school seals itself for the night and the power fails. The dead children move through the halls, gentle but insistent, repeating the hymn's missing verses. Ruth demands Juniper burn the ledger. The beat is siege pressure: the truth is trying to get in, and the lie is trying to burn.

chapters.title: Verses the Living Forgot
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Trapped in the archive room, Juniper reads the ledger aloud as the dead children gather, and the incomplete hymn completes itself through the room. Ada shows Juniper the last verse: a name—the elders who locked the mill door. The beat is revelation as mercy: the children don't want revenge. They want to be counted.

chapters.title: The Door Answers Back
chapters.summary: Climax. Juniper, Dale, and Marisol fight through the dark school to the cellar door as the thing the elders invited in—keeper of the buried crime—rises to collect its debt. Ruth Kettle, confronted with the ledger and the verse bearing her name, chooses confession over sacrifice and walks down to the door herself. The beat is terrible justice outside any law.

chapters.title: Sunrise Roll Call
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, dawn. The children, counted and named, pass through the open door and are gone; the thing below accepts Ruth and closes. Juniper files the real record with the county, names all eleven in the town paper, and keeps teaching—eleven desks removed at last. The final beat is quiet belonging: some prayers are answered by being written down.
